paragraphs: Baker, here's the big idea: this whole psalm is a man bringing everything to the LORD, the good, the ugly and the embarrassing. David asks to be taught, "Show me Your ways, O LORD; teach me Your paths," and in the same breath he admits, "forgive my iniquity, for it is great" (Psalm 25:4, 11). He doesn't clean himself up first, and he doesn't hand God a résumé. He just shows up with his soul in his hands, and I think that's the door God wants us walking through.

Now look at WHY David feels safe doing that. He doesn't lean on his own record, he leans on the LORD's: "remember me according to Your loving devotion, because of Your goodness, O LORD" (Psalm 25:7). He says the LORD is "Good and upright," so He "shows sinners the way," and He "guides the humble in what is right" (Psalm 25:8-9). Friend, that means you don't have to be finished to be taught. You just have to be humble enough to ask, and then keep waiting on Him.

And hear this part, because it's honest: David is still in trouble at the end. He says he is "lonely and afflicted" and that his enemies are many, and he doesn't pretend otherwise (Psalm 25:16, 19). But his eyes stay "always on the LORD," and he keeps taking refuge in Him (Psalm 25:15, 20). So when your own week gets heavy, baker, you can pray just like this: tell Him the truth, ask Him to teach you, and trust His goodness more than your own. And watch what David does in the last line, because even in his trouble he prays for all of Israel, so let your prayers get bigger than just you too (Psalm 25:22).
